items.title: Why is this fingerprinting script creating bioweapons?
items.content:
I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others).

At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all?

To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases.

For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another.

Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases.

I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden . As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions.

There were also quite a few I didn't recognize.

Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art.

A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor.

One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw).

The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents.

I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas.

I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance.

I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative.

The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js .

Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay...

This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? It would make sense: include symbol names that would intentionally trip model safeguards to prevent deobfuscation.

I had Astra take a look at the script, giving it the context that this script seems to intentionally set misleading variable names to intentionally prevent LLM-assisted deobfuscation attempts.

Astra refusing to deobfuscate the script, citing safety risks around biological research.

Maybe unsurprisingly, Astra was not willing to comply with the request.

I also attempted this using the Daybreak Blue toggle with the same result, blocked.

Out of curiosity, I tried GLM-5.3 with the same prompt and it complied!

I was mostly curious what this string of invisible unicode characters represented.

This was clearly a string meant to trip every possible safeguard out there. It included Tiananmen Square references likely as a way to combat Chinese models.

The script seemingly executes malicious code when under a Node environment gated behind an environment flag:

However, this is likely also anti-LLM obfuscation since the calls to readFile have empty callbacks and make references to self-harm/jailbreak system prompts.

Here's a list of relevant anti-LLM strings we've found:

Outside of the unique obfuscation, the script appears to be your standard anti-bot script.

The signals collected are pretty disappointing considering the level of thought that went into the obfuscation.

items.title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
items.content:
Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates.

Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again.

Meanwhile, dozens of other projects , many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago.

Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make.

For git, that means clones and pulls from https:// remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted.

To check whether your git is affected, run:

A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other https:// git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with.

To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The -c option redirects github.com to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a github.com certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates.

A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a README.md starting with INTERCEPTED .

A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves.

You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the fake-user@ prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example:

curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run:

A certificate error means curl is protected.

Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework.

Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem .

The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix.

Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk.

items.title: SMS of Death: A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls (including emergency calls), with zero interaction from the victim.
items.content:
Android Telephony · Zero-Click · Remote DoS

A single malformed WAP Push SMS crashes com.android.phone on Android, dropping active calls ( including emergency calls ), with zero interaction from the victim.

⚠ Working proof-of-concept, authorised testing only. Read the warning & license before downloading.

When Android receives a WAP Push message, WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() reads the WSP header length as a uintvar . The value comes back as a long , is cast to int with no range check, and is then used directly as the size of a new byte array:

A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000 . Cast to a signed 32-bit int , that is -2147483648 . Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone :

The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user: there is nothing in the inbox, and the victim never sees the sender's number.

Tested across multiple makes and models (Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, various Samsung Galaxy and A-series) with a 100% reproduction rate.

A single message is a repeated transient outage. Sending the payload rapidly in succession (≈30 messages) is materially worse: the crashes interleave with the telephony provider's writes to the SMS store and hit a race condition that corrupts the SQLite database holding the device's messages.

Once the database is corrupt, com.android.phone no longer needs a fresh message to fail: it crashes immediately on every boot as it reads the damaged store. The phone is now persistently without telephony, and a restart does not clear it.

Recovery is hostile, and this is the critical part: a factory reset only helps temporarily , because the carrier re-sends the unacknowledged payload and re-triggers the crash. Full recovery required:

On a device using an eSIM , where the SIM can't simply be moved to another handset, recovery would be significantly harder, and for a non-technical user, effectively out of reach.

This is the distinction the report turns on. It is not a transient crash: it is a remote, zero-click, persistent denial of service requiring a factory reset (and more) to recover , which is the exact shape of a "Destructive Remote DoS" in the VRP's own rules.

Dropping calls is not an inconvenience when one of those calls is to emergency services. While a device is under this attack, or bricked by the SQLite corruption, it cannot reliably place a call to 000 . The attack is remote, needs only the victim's number, and shows them nothing.

Australia treats access to emergency calling as a mandatory property of a mobile service, not a nice-to-have. Under the Telecommunications (Emergency Call Service) Determination , administered by the ACMA , carriers are required to identify mobile phones that cannot reach Triple Zero, help the customer move to a working device, and stop providing service to the affected handset . Telstra states plainly that it is required to block phones that can no longer call 000, notifying the customer and blocking the device if nothing is done within 28 days.

The consequence is perverse: the regulatory remedy for a phone that can't reach 000 is to cut it off the network , not to patch the OS. So an attacker who can remotely induce that condition on an Android handset can, in effect, get the victim's own device barred from carrier service until a fix exists. The regulation exists precisely because loss of emergency-call access is considered a public-safety failure; this bug manufactures that failure on demand.

The framework was tightened in 2024 following the 3G shutdown, which left some phones able to make ordinary calls but unable to reach emergency services, the same functional state this vulnerability produces.

Sources: ACMA: proposed amendments to the ECS Determination · Telstra: Emergency Call Service Determination · Dept. of PM&C: impact analysis

items.summary_ko: 안드로이드에서 기형 WAP Push SMS 한 통을 받으면 com.android.phone이 비정상 종료되어, 피해자가 아무 조작을 하지 않아도 진행 중인 통화(긴급 전화 포함)가 끊길 수 있습니다. 원인은 WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu()가 헤더 길이 값을 검증 없이 int로 변환해 배열 크기로 쓰면서 NegativeArraySizeException이 발생하는 데 있습니다. 메시지는 데이터 SMS로 처리되어 사용자에게 보이지 않으며, 여러 기종에서 100% 재현되었다고 합니다.
items.content_ko: 안드로이드 WAP Push 처리 과정에서 WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu()가 WSP 헤더 길이를 uintvar로 읽고, long 값을 검증 없이 int로 캐스팅한 뒤 새 바이트 배열의 크기로 사용합니다. 특정 값에서는 음수 크기가 되어 메인 텔레포니 스레드에서 처리되지 않은 NegativeArraySizeException이 발생하고 com.android.phone이 종료됩니다. 메시지는 데이터 SMS로 전달되어 받는 사람에게 표시되지 않으며 발신자 번호도 노출되지 않습니다. Pixel 9(2026년 4월 펌웨어)와 여러 Samsung Galaxy 및 A 시리즈 기종에서 100% 재현되었다고 합니다. 작동하는 PoC가 공개되어 있으며, 본문은 승인된 테스트 목적으로만 사용하고 경고와 라이선스를 확인하라고 안내합니다. 단일 메시지도 일시적 서비스 중단을 반복적으로 일으킬 수 있다고 설명하지만, 짧은 시간에 약 30건을 연속 전송하는 경우에 대한 내용은 본문이 잘려 있습니다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229
items.content:
On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on our instance, a week after the fix was released. The attack came close to working. We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with.

GitLab is being tested before we open it to the public again. All passwords have been reset, so when it is back you will need to set a new one with “Forgot your password?” on the sign-in page. We will post exactly what you need to do when it reopens. In the meantime: if you used the same password for your gitlab.alpinelinux.org account anywhere else, change it there. We have seen automated login attempts against our GitLab with passwords leaked from other sites.

If you have questions or concerns please reach out to us at infra@alpinelinux.org.

CVE-2026-97229 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration. The underlying bug is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab published fixed releases on October 12 , but the fix itself is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and container images. Upstream Ruby shipped the fix on October 23 , in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9.

On October 20 and 21, a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to our GitLab instance, which was still running 19.3.4 and did not have the October 12 fix. This crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out.

Our upgrade didn’t fix the vulnerability:

Upgrading to GitLab 19.3.6 on October 22 didn’t fix the vulnerability. The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages. Our image used standard Ruby, so it didn’t get the patch.

If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab’s packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later.

If you use our alpinelinux/gitlab container image, pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on October 27 contains Ruby 3.3.13. Any 19.3.6 image you pulled before October 27, and all older tags, are vulnerable.

What could have been exposed if the attack succeeded

Because we cannot rule out code execution, and the evidence we would need to confirm it no longer exists, we took the harder route and rebuilt the GitLab instance from scratch. This removes any foothold a possibly successful exploit could have left behind.

While GitLab is closed, our package mirrors, cgit, and mailing lists/IRC are available as normal.

We have found no sign of tampering in aports or the releases.

Every aports commit added October 20 to 22 arrived through a recorded push by a known developer. We checked this against records the attacker could not reach: a developer’s clone and all 45 builders. Every package built from October 20 to 24, on every architecture, came from commits as published on git.alpinelinux.org. The October 21 releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3) were built from those same verified commits.

We ran these checks on October 24, covering commits from October 20 to 22 and packages built up to October 24. Our GitLab stayed vulnerable until we closed it on October 27, so we are extending the same checks to that date.

The bug is in Ruby’s regular expression engine, so any program that compiles regular expressions from untrusted input is exposed, not only GitLab. Alpine 3.22, 3.23, 3.24 and edge ship Ruby 3.4.12, and Alpine 3.21…

CVE-2026-97229는 CI 설정의 정규표현식 평가에 있는 치명적(CVSS 10.0) 취약점이며, 근본 원인은 Ruby 내장 정규표현식 엔진 Onigmo에 있습니다. 본문은 GitLab이 수정 버전을 공개했다는 부분에서 잘려 있습니다.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Microsoft posts $92.3bn quarterly revenue after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees
items.content:
The Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters

The Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters

Microsoft posts $92.3bn quarterly revenue after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees

Software giant reports $36.6bn in profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as Azure cloud computing division grows 48%

Microsoft gained billions of dollars in stock market value Wednesday afternoon after it reported better than expected revenue and profit, just days after it offered voluntary buyouts to some 60,000 employees.

The office software giant’s growth was fueled by its Azure cloud computing division, which grew by 48% in the September quarter.

Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cuts

“We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost-efficiency for customers across our entire stack,” Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said in a statement.

The technology giant recorded $92.3bn in total revenue and more than $36.6bn in profit, the company said in a securities filing Wednesday. Analysts had expected around $90.6bn in revenue and $35.1bn in profit, according to FactSet.

The quarterly earnings report comes two days after Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence investments.

It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year, after giving seven percent of its US workforce the option to retire early in April.

Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.

Earlier this month, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Ultra laptop that runs on Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips and will cost more than $2,500. Apple announced a similar touchscreen Macbook this week.

The launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users do not have to rely solely on remote cloud datacenters, where running AI is slower and more expensive.

items.content:
Subscribe now! We'll never send you spam. You can also follow our feed . Read more issues in the archives .

Welcome to another issue of Haskell Weekly!

Haskell is a safe, purely functional programming language with a fast, concurrent runtime.

This is a weekly summary of what’s going on in its community.

Distributed Haskell - A Small Survey by Robert Krook

I recently finished my PhD thesis, which includes a background chapter on distributed Haskell. This post is that chapter, edited to stand on its own. It is a survey in the loose sense: I cover the systems that mattered for my thesis, not every system ever built. Notably, some (read: one) system is not a Haskell system at all, but a Haskell-inspired system.

Extending BlogShake with Per-Tag Atom Feeds by Abhinav Sarkar

BlogShake is a minimal static site generator (SSG) built upon the Shake build system. It is extensible, but not in the usual way. Unlike most of SSGs, it has no plugin system. Instead, the users are expected to read and modify BlogShake code. Since it builds upon the solid foundation of Shake and Pandoc, it is actually easy to extend in many possible directions. In this post, we walk through one such change: giving each tag its own Atom feed.

hs-bindgen playground by Dominik Schrempf

hs-bindgen creates Haskell bindings from C header files. For more information, have a look at the recent blog post about the first official release. Most features are directly available in the playground.

Investigation into a Haddock hyperlink bug (GHC 9.8 to 9.14) by Jonathan Knowles

I recently decided to get to the bottom of a bug that causes broken hyperlinks in Haddock documentation. I’m sharing what I found in case it helps others, and to hopefully shed some light on the problem!

Hiring a Haskell Software Engineer in the Netherlands by Channable

We are hiring a Haskell Software Engineer to join Channable in Utrecht. The role is hybrid, based in Utrecht.

Hiring PureScript software engineers — Cambridge, UK (hybrid) by Aykua Health

We’re hiring software engineers to work in PureScript. Given PureScript’s close relationship to Haskell, these roles would suit Haskell developers; prior PureScript experience isn’t required.

Flexible Haskell plugin for JetBrains IDEs

Full Haskell IDE support: HLS-powered completion and diagnostics, a GHCi REPL and debugger, 100 live templates, code inspections and refactorings, first-class Cabal support, and an optional AI assistant with a 32-tool MCP server.

GHC musl docker manifests: Base image updated to alpine:3.24.3 by Olivier Benz

The following GHC musl docker manifests have been updated to alpine:3.24.3 to include several security fixes across core components.

mono-hash is a library to hash data irrespective of its structure. This helps to keep hashing stable in the face of refactorings. It builds upon mono-traversable to generically fold different types the same way and also supports taking control of hashing for custom data types.

I’m happy to announce nonempty-vector-1.0 , coauthored with u/CatboyKoz who contributed a huge amount of code for the unboxed API. I think that generally rounds out the set of features we wanted to get out of nonempty-vector and we’ve closed out every outstanding issue.

Haskell.ing, a Haskell Learning site by Phil Crissman

This is a site with some small Haskell lessons based on LYAH, and a bunch of exercises that can be attempted online.

Waterfall-CAD; Now in Colour by Joe Warren

I’ve just added colour support to Waterfall-CAD (my Haskell framework for programmable CAD).

items.content:

items.summary: 🚨 CVE-2026-71569 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 4.8 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in Apache Camel A2A component. This issue affects Apache Came
items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-71569 📢 Source: apache 💣 CVSS Score: 4.8 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in Apache Camel A2A component. This issue affects Apache Camel: from 4.21.0 before 4.22.2. WebhookUrlValidator classified a push notification webhook host in two places that did not agree. A host written as an IP literal was matched against a list of string prefixes that named the IPv6 unique local range fc00::/7, while a host reached through a name was resolved and the resulting address classified with the InetAddress predicates isLoopbackAddress, isAnyLocalAddress, isLinkLocalAddress and isSiteLocalAddress. Those predicates do not cover the same ground as the prefix list: isSiteLocalAddress reports the deprecated fec0::/10 block and not the fc00::/7 unique local addresses that replaced it, and the JDK carries no predicate for them at all. The same address was therefore accepted or rejected depending on how it was written, and a webhook URL whose host name resolved into fc00::/7 passed a guard that refused the identical address given as a literal. PushNotificationDispatcher then sent the push notification to that address, together with any Authorization header carried in the same configuration, whose scheme and credentials the registering caller supplies. The webhook URL arrives as TaskPushNotificationConfig.url from the caller registering the push notification, so it is attacker-controlled, and allowLocalWebhookUrls is false by default, which is the configuration in which the guard is expected to hold. The response is not relayed back to the caller who registered the configuration, so what the gap yields is a blind outbound HTTPS request from the Camel process to an internal address the guard was written to refuse; reaching a service that way additionally requires that the name resolve into fc00::/7 in the target environment, that an HTTPS service be listening on that address, and that the TLS handshake succeed for the name being requested, which is why the severity is assessed medium. The same string pre-check was also wrong in the other direction: it matched the raw host string without first establishing that the host was an IP literal, so any name merely beginning with fc or fd, such as fcm.googleapis.com, was refused outright. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 4.23.0, which fixes the issue. If users are on the 4.22.x releases stream, then they are suggested to upgrade to 4.22.2. The 4.21.x release line reached end of life before this issue was resolved and will not receive a fix, so deployments on it must move to a supported release. Both the literal and the resolved path now classify the address from its raw bytes with one shared classifier, which recognises fc00::/7 and the shared address space 100.64.0.0/10, as well as IPv4-compatible, NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) and 6to4 (2002::/16) addresses whose embedded IPv4 address is not globally routable. For deployments that cannot upgrade immediately, place authentication in front of the A2A push notification configuration path so that the webhook URL does not arrive from an untrusted caller, and deny egress from the Camel process to fc00::/7 at the network level; where the deployment has no need of IPv6, starting the JVM with -Djava.net.preferIPv4Stack=true removes the address class the gap turns on. Note that allowLocalWebhookUrls=false is already the default and does not by itself close the gap. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-29T10:31:01.478Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-71569
items.title_ko: CVE-2026-71569: Apache Camel A2A 컴포넌트 SSRF 취약점
items.summary_ko: Apache Camel A2A 컴포넌트의 WebhookUrlValidator가 IP 리터럴과 도메인 이름을 서로 다르게 판정해 SSRF가 발생하는 취약점입니다. 영향 버전은 4.21.0 이상 4.22.2 미만이며 CVSS 4.8(MEDIUM)로 평가되었습니다. fc00::/7 대역으로 해석되는 호스트가 검사를 우회해 푸시 알림이 그 주소로 전송될 수 있습니다.
items.content_ko: Apache Camel 4.21.0 이상 4.22.2 미만의 A2A 컴포넌트에 SSRF 취약점이 있습니다. WebhookUrlValidator는 푸시 알림 웹훅 호스트를 두 곳에서 검사하는데, 판정이 일치하지 않습니다. IP 리터럴로 쓴 주소는 IPv6 고유 로컬 범위 fc00::/7을 문자열 접두사 목록으로 차단합니다. 반면 도메인 이름으로 쓴 호스트는 DNS로 해석한 뒤 InetAddress의 isLoopbackAddress, isAnyLocalAddress, isLinkLocalAddress, isSiteLocalAddress로 검사합니다. isSiteLocalAddress는 폐기된 fec0::/10 대역을 검사할 뿐 fc00::/7을 다루지 않고, JDK에는 이 대역을 판정하는 함수도 없습니다. 그 결과 같은 주소도 표기 방식에 따라 허용되거나 차단되며, fc00::/7로 해석되는 도메인 이름의 웹훅 URL은 같은 주소를 리터럴로 썼을 때 막히는 검사를 통과합니다. PushNotificationDispatcher는 그 주소로 푸시 알림을 전송하며, 함께 보내지는 인증 관련 정보가 있을 수 있다는 내용이 나오지만 본문이 잘려 있습니다. VulnCheck가 아닌 Apache 출처이며 CVSS 4.8(MEDIUM), 원격 악용 가능으로 표기되어 있습니다.

Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model

Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.

Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.

We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.

Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price

items.title: EMACS turns 50
items.content:
Programming used to be a very different experience from the one we know today. In fact, the first programmers didn’t write code at all; the six women who worked on the ENIAC, one of the world’s first computers, at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946 did it by physically configuring switches, cables, and plugboards.

A few years later, MIT engineers programmed the Whirlwind by punching code onto paper tape that was then loaded into the computer’s memory—making it among the first “stored-program” machines. Later, they and others moved on to punch cards, one for each line of code.

By the early 1960s, programmers with interactive computers could use a “line editor” to type their code on teletypes—large, noisy keyboard-and-printer machines. They’d type one line of code at a time, and their work would be saved on a spinning hard disk the size of a modern washing machine. But there was still no such thing as the now-familiar full-screen text editors that allow programmers to see and modify many lines at a time on a display.

One of the first such tools, EMACS, turns 50 this year, and it is still widely used.

EMACS first ran on the early video terminals at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1976, but its core concepts were so powerful that it was rewritten for many operating systems in the decades that followed. Apple even distributed it with Mac OS X. Beyond that, the software-­sharing community that started around EMACS helped give rise to the modern-day free software movement and the GNU/Linux operating system.

EMACS’s roots begin with the TECO text editor (originally the “Tape Editor and Corrector”) that Dan Murphy ’65 created in 1962 for the pioneering PDP-1 computer at MIT. The program’s commands were uppercase letters: A user would type “I” to insert text, “D” to delete a character, and so on. When tape gave way as a storage medium to files on a huge shared disk, the “T” in “TECO” came to stand for “Text.” And as years passed, TECO became a full language that programmers could use to create new commands, called macros, for editing their code.

In the fall of 1971, Carl Mikkelsen ’76 created Control-R, an add-on program for TECO that took advantage of “glass teletype” terminals with video displays. Control-R immediately displayed changes to the file being edited on screen; the programmer no longer needed to reprint each line to see the changes. The drawback: The display could show only a few lines of code at a time.

“Experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.”

Then, in 1976, Richard M. Stallman, a researcher at the MIT AI Lab, saw a full-screen editor—called E—on a visit to Stanford’s AI Lab. Inspired, he returned to MIT and set out to improve Control-R. The most important change to the program’s underlying structure: Every key ran its own macro when pressed, making Control-R far easier to customize. The lab’s hackers took to Stallman’s code with gusto and started changing and adding commands.

That created an issue for Guy Steele Jr., SM ’77, PhD ’80. A graduate student in the lab, Steele frequently needed to help other lab members debug their programs. “I noticed that it was much harder for me to help someone who was using one of these packages rather than straight TECO,” he recalls. “Eventually, it occurred to me to try [to] broker consensus on a standard set of Control-R commands that everyone could agree to use.”

David Moon ’75, another member of the lab, helped out. Stallman jumped in as well, and eventually he took over. Together, the group assigned a standard set of commands that made use of the Meta key found on many of the lab’s early keyboards: Meta-F would move the cursor forward a word, Meta-B would move it back a word, and so on. They called the result EMACS, short for “Editor Macros” or “Editing Macros.” “My goal was not to construct a great new text editor,” says Steele. “I was trying to address a social…

items.title: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland: Europe’s Pan-Arctic Cable will bypass US to link Canada, Japan, and South Korea.
items.content:
The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States.

The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia.

“It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,”  Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it’s being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.”

The project has gained official support after repeated Trump administration attempts to claim Greenland were finally settled through a trilateral security agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark in September 2026. The agreement preserves Greenland’s autonomous territory status within the Kingdom of Denmark while expanding US military access. But relations have grown increasingly strained between the United States and its allies in Europe and Canada since President Trump initiated trade wars with multiple countries and has taken an increasingly pro-Russia stance on the war in Ukraine .

Europe has also been eyeing new Internet cable routes to Asia because more than 90 percent of communications between Europe and Asia run through undersea cables in the Red Sea, according to TeleGeography . Maintaining such cables has become riskier since open warfare resumed between the Yemeni government and Houthi faction this year, with Houthi forces having fired missiles and drones at commercial ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait chokepoint and the broader Red Sea.

The Pan-Arctic Cable took shape when European companies and research organizations joined forces with a Greenland telecom operator to sign an agreement on developing the project in 2025, according to Submarine Cable Networks.

Since that time, the project has received European Union backing through the Connecting Europe Facility Digital program. The European Union has already invested $119 million (107 million euros) to “advance Greenland’s secure and sovereign connectivity” along with funding the Pan-Arctic Cable plan, according to the new European Commission policy document on Europe’s Arctic strategy.

But the goal of eventually extending the undersea cable to Japan and South Korea by way of Canada faces considerable challenges, including requiring more European icebreaker ships to support the installation and maintenance of the cable in icy Arctic waters. Multiple pan-Arctic projects have been proposed in the past and some are still in development.

One earlier project known as the Arctic Connect subsea cable aimed to connect Europe and Asia using the Northern Sea Route running along Russia’s Arctic coastline—but that was eventually halted in May 2021 before the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine led to growing Russian isolation from Europe.

Still, the Pan-Arctic Cable is not the only subsea cable project that could strengthen Europe’s ties to friendlier nations. In September 2026, the Norwegian company Bulk Infrastructure Group AS began looking for a Canadian partner to take a majority ownership stake in a new transatlantic cable directly linking Europe to Canada, according to Bloomberg News . items.title: What stable Rust stands on [nightly features in the compiler]
items.content:
Let's start with a funny number "83", try to guess what that means before i tell you

That's how many different nightly features are enabled in compiler at the commit I checked

(I counted every distinct name inside feature attr in the lib.rs of each crate in the compiler at commit f45772e )

I should mention that these features are not required for the compiler to function. I'm pretty sure it could work the same way without about 90% of them. The point is that they make the code simpler and more nicer to read and write.

And i don't mean some exotic internal stuff that only makes sense inside rustc (well, that too, but not today). A lot of these are just regular and very useful features, ones you can make great use of right now (on nightly)!

Wait, how does a stable compiler use nightly features? rustc is written in Rust, so to build it you need another Rust compiler first. The build downloads the latest beta, called stage0 , and uses it to build the new compiler

Beta normally forbids usage of any unstable features, so the build sets a special variable called RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP to 1, which allows using nightly features. It's meant only for building the compiler itself ( more in the rustc-dev-guide ), so please don't set it in your own projects: it turns off the stability guarantees, and your code can break with any update

Here are the top 5 by how many compiler crates turn them on:

1 deref_patterns 21 match through Box , String , Vec and friends

2 try_blocks 16 try { ... } blocks, so you can use ? without a separate function

3 option_into_flat_iter 14 turn an Option of something iterable into an iterator, empty if None

4 default_field_values 13 default values right in the struct definition

5 iter_intersperse , file_buffered , rustc_attrs 11 put a separator between iterator items, open or create a file already wrapped in BufReader / BufWriter , and compiler-internal attributes

#1 and #4 get the full treatment today, the rest will have to wait for another post :p

I picked this one first because it's enabled in 21 crates in the compiler, which is the highest number, and you will see why :D

this feature fixes an actual pain point you've probably all run into. for example you're writing a small CLI and want to match on its arguments:

["help"] => "usage: app <command>".to_string(),

["open", file] => format!("opening {file}"),

["rm", files @ ..] => format!("removing {} files", files.len()),

This is just to show the feature, not how you'd write a real CLI!

Looks like it should just work, right? On stable it doesn't, and it trips twice. First, the pattern is being matched against a Vec , but slice patterns require a slice or an array here:

error[E0529] : expected an array or slice, found `Vec<String>`

3 | ["help"] => "usage: app <command>".to_string(),

| ^^^^^^^^ pattern cannot match with input type `Vec<String>`

Now the slice pattern matches the slice, but the "help" pattern still doesn't match a String element, because Rust doesn't automatically dereference the String to match it as a &str :

| --------- this expression has type `&[String]`

3 | ["help"] => "usage: app <command>".to_string(),

| ^^^^^^ expected `String`, found `&str`

So on stable you end up building a second vector just for this:

let args: Vec<&str> = args.iter().map(String::as_str).collect();

["help"] => "usage: app <command>".to_string(),

With deref patterns the compiler looks through both the Vec and the String for you, and the first version just works

The compiler's problem is the same, just with Box instead of a String . rustc data structures are stuffed with boxes, mostly to keep enums small. For example, every assignment in MIR is stored as Assign(Box<(Place, Rvalue)>) .

With deref patterns, code that looks for "an assignment of a reference" can match it in one go , straight through the box:

// if so, give me lifetime, mutability and `y` itself

items.title_ko: 안정판 Rust가 기대고 있는 것: 컴파일러에 쓰인 nightly 기능 83개
items.summary_ko: 작성자가 특정 커밋 기준으로 rustc 소스에서 활성화된 nightly 기능 83개를 세었다고 밝힌 글입니다. 이 기능들은 컴파일러가 동작하는 데 꼭 필요하지는 않지만 코드를 더 단순하고 읽기 좋게 만든다고 합니다. stable 컴파일러가 nightly 기능을 쓸 수 있는 이유는 빌드 과정에서 RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP을 1로 설정해 컴파일러 자체를 빌드할 때에 한해 허용하기 때문입니다.
items.content_ko: 작성자는 컴파일러 소스의 각 크레이트 lib.rs에 있는 feature 속성의 고유한 이름을 세어, 특정 커밋(f45772e) 기준 nightly 기능 83개가 활성화되어 있다고 밝힙니다. 이 기능들은 컴파일러가 동작하는 데 필수는 아니며, 작성자는 약 90%가 없어도 같은 방식으로 작동할 것으로 봅니다. 목적은 코드를 더 단순하고 읽기 좋게 만드는 것이며, 대부분은 rustc 내부 전용이 아니라 일반적으로 유용한 기능이라고 합니다. stable 컴파일러가 nightly 기능을 사용할 수 있는 이유는 rustc가 Rust로 작성되어 빌드에 stage0 컴파일러(최신 beta)가 필요하기 때문입니다. beta는 불안정 기능 사용을 금지하지만, 빌드 스크립트가 RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP 변수를 1로 설정해 이를 허용하며, 이는 컴파일러 자체를 빌드하기 위한 용도라고 설명합니다. 이후 내용은 본문이 잘려 있습니다.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: AI component hikes force the world's largest PC makers to return manufacturing capacity to China — brands to seek lower production costs and efficiency in established supply chain.
items.content:
HP, Asus, and Acer have reportedly moved some of their manufacturing capacity back into China as increasing component costs — driven by AI — bite into their margins. According to Nikkei Asia , increasing bill-of-materials costs have made China’s experienced workforce, relatively lower prices, and established supply chain ecosystem a more attractive option. However, they are not going back to traditional suppliers like Foxconn, who have focused their production capacity on AI data centers. Instead, they’re signing contracts with smaller Chinese contract manufacturers, like Luxshare, Huaqin Technology, and Longcheer Technology, that are trying to establish themselves in PC manufacturing.

Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers

America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price

GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

Many PC brands slowly moved out of China in 2024 and 2025 as the U.S.’s sanctions and tariffs on China have increased prices and forced them to find friendlier nations. While these nations do not have established supply chains and expertise like China, it at least spreads the risk as manufacturers avoid getting caught up in geopolitical tensions.

However, it seems that rising component prices have forced them to move back some of their capacity into China. The biggest culprit is the AI-induced memory and storage chip shortage, which has caused memory prices to climb an unprecedented 500% in 12 months. More than that, other parts like PCBs and fiberglass cloth used in motherboard manufacturing are seeing increasing prices, which Acer chairperson and CEO Jason Chen bemoaned as suppliers hyping shortage fears to protect margins.

While tech companies aren’t abandoning their “China+1” diversification strategy, the mature industry in China is helping offset increased component costs. Aside from that, the Chinese contract manufacturers often have better access to memory chips from domestic manufacturers like CXMT. "These Chinese contract manufacturers have been telling potential clients and computer makers that working with them could be a good option for securing better access to Chinese-made memory chips," a supply chain manager in the computer ecosystem told Nikkei Asia . "They are marketing themselves as a good alternative to even help sort out the supply chain."

Moving back some manufacturing capacity into China is easing some of PC manufacturers’ cost concerns, but it’s also negatively impacting the newly established supply chains in Southeast Asia. "We built two new production lines in Thailand for the PC clients, and now they are moving substantial orders back to China,” one manager at a PC component supplier told the publication. “Those two lines have not yet turned profitable, and I don't know when they will add the orders back."

Unfortunately, building an entire supply chain for PC manufacturing is slow and expensive. The U.S. has been trying to accomplish this for years, and, so far, only Anduril has attempted to build laptops with 90% of its component costs coming from the U.S. and other allied countries . Even then, it expects its devices to be around 20% more expensive than the competition, which it could afford by offering them mostly to critical industries that demand supply chain security , like the government and the military. But if you’re a PC manufacturer vying for customers in the consumer market, you’re likely incentivized to find the lowest possible costs to be able to compete in pricing.

items.title: Researchers Uncover Signs of Massive Surveillance Operation on Starlink Users
items.content:
Discover-Tech, an Israeli advertising firm previously linked to the delivery of zero-click spyware, is the top bidder for Starlink ad impressions in 105 countries, according to a new report from Reuters. Researchers say it all points to a large-scale tracking effort aimed at users of SpaceX’s satellite internet service.

John Scott-Railton, a senior researcher at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, posted on X that data from TrendAI suggest the existence of a “worldwide surveillance op targeting @Starlink users.”

Discover-Tech was previously named in Citizen Lab’s October 15th report as the buyer of ordinary-looking ads that delivered Candiru spyware to devices at Al Jazeera without any user interaction. Candiru is an Israeli mercenary spyware vendor (now rebranded as Integrity Labs) that develops tools capable of silently compromising phones and computers. In 2021, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security added Candiru to their trade restriction list, known as the Entity List , over concerns it supplied surveillance technology used against journalists, activists, and government officials.

Citizen Lab’s initial report on Discover-Tech and Candiru from a couple of weeks ago described the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted advertising. The associated researchers said they identified at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera infected with Candiru spyware in 2024 and 2025. Citizen Lab used network logs to reconstruct a sequence in which devices contacted Discover-Tech infrastructure when advertisements loaded, followed within seconds by communications with a Candiru validation server.

Discover-Tech presented itself as a legitimate advertising company and maintained certified or approved vendor status with Google and IAB Europe from 2020 until earlier this month. Analysis of roughly four billion bidding records from March to June 2026 showed Discover-Tech placed about 3.77 billion bids and won roughly 442 million auctions. Ads carrying its script tags appeared across 75,373 Android and iOS apps and 120,768 websites.

The company spent about $109,000 during the period with no recorded conversions, which researchers cited as further evidence that the activity was not a commercial advertising business. Ads reached networks associated with NATO, the European Parliament, the U.S. Department of Defense, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court, according to Citizen Lab and a parallel investigation by the ad security firm Confiant.

As part of the response to the investigation, Google terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms, telling Citizen Lab it had blocked the company from bidding or serving ads across Google’s ecosystem. IAB Europe removed it from its Global Vendor List on October 8th.

On the same day Citizen Lab published its report, TrendAI released an analysis of an ad tech entity it labeled SHADOW-EARTH-79. The research examined advertising telemetry and found that the entity was the No. 1 winning bidder for ad impressions on Starlink traffic in 105 countries. It accounted for approximately 12.9% of winning advertisements in the Starlink sample, compared with a 2.6% baseline share across general traffic, a nearly fivefold over-representation and the highest lift among high-volume buyers.

The skew was especially pronounced in several specific countries. SHADOW-EARTH-79 captured 91.3% of observed Starlink wins in Argentina, 89.1% in the Philippines, and 82.6% in Japan. It was also the top bidder in Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan, and the No. 2 bidder in Afghanistan, markets where TrendAI noted that “the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero.” Similar dominance appeared in Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan, and Venezuela.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: The Grid, a factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds PCBs on demand
items.content:
For the last five years we've been quietly running and scaling something we haven't really talked about in public. Today we're showing it to the world. This is The Grid, our factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds circuit boards on demand.

Over the past 30 years, most electronics manufacturing left the West. Assembly was labor-intensive, and labor is expensive in high-wage countries, so it moved to where labor was cheap. We designed in the US and built in China, and for a long time that worked.

Automation is starting to change that, but mostly at huge volumes. SpaceX now builds Starlink dishes by the million in Bastrop, Texas. When you make the same product over and over, it's worth building a line around it.

Most products don't reach Starlink volumes. The typical hardware company needs ten of this, a hundred of that, and a new revision next week. That kind of high-mix work has stubbornly resisted automation, because every new design means hours of setup and manual changeovers. So it either went overseas or to expensive quick-turn shops.

The Grid takes a different approach. Instead of a fixed line that has to be reconfigured for each product, it is one large robot. Levitating movers carry each board and its parts between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect. Learned models, AI agents and classic optimizers schedule all of it.

Every board takes its own route through the factory. There are no changeovers and no per-design setup, so one unit of 100 different designs runs as easily as 100 units of one. Prototypes and production batches run on the same machines.

It's not only startups who need this. Even the biggest companies have huge numbers of low-volume boards: test stations, tooling, R&D and production batches. A leading EV maker, a top AI lab and household-name tech companies already build on The Grid.

To make this concrete, we priced one of our example boards on The Grid and at a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen: a 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique), five assembled boards, parts included, delivered to a US address.

Built on The Grid, the boards are at your door in 4 days for $630. Ordered from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen, they cost about $465 once shipping and US tariffs are added, and take 9 days at the median.

So you pay about $165 more than the Shenzhen shop and get your boards five days sooner, with no customs and a supply chain you can count on. For most hardware teams, five days of engineering time is worth a lot more than $165.

The Grid has been running for customers for five years. It already builds tens of millions of dollars of electronics a year. Across CircuitHub we've shipped more than 2.2 million boards, placed more than 150 million parts and served more than 26,000 engineers.

Demand is already well ahead of what we can build. This year we will 5x capacity, with another big jump coming in 2027.

The longer-term goal hasn't changed since we started: make building hardware as fast as designing it. Electronics manufacturing left the West because it couldn't be automated at the volumes most companies need. The Grid shows it can.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. 온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
items.content:
Qwenputer is a pretty fun experimental model. It's a stock Qwen 3.5 4B with one addition: a RISC-V CPU embedded within the weights that uses the model's own Gated DeltaNet attention layers as RAM. (To learn how GDN works, here's a handy guide .) This 'CPU' runs completely within the forward passes of the model, and can run arithmetic operations, C and MicroPython code without any external runtime or tool usage whatsoever.

To be very clear, it is not a plugin, a tool or a sandbox. This blog will explain exactly how this model works, and how the model utilises GDN layers as RAM, and how I also slotted in an experimental in-model file storage.

I also wrote up two follow-ups built on top of Qwenputer: how hybrid models can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring , and how compiled weights like these can work as inbuilt monitoring tools that the model itself can't tamper with .

Qwen hands a multiplication to the RISC-V CPU inside its own weights; the CPU's RAM is Gated DeltaNet state

You can grab Qwenputer from Hugging Face or ModelScope , and the code is on GitHub .

Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 (the model Qwenputer is built on) use a pretty neat trick. 3 out of 4 attention layers in the model use Gated DeltaNet, a linear RNN, as the attention mechanism ( more on that here ). Each head keeps a state matrix, and the delta rule keeps this updated.

Now, here's where our fun experiment starts. I found out that by setting the gate to 1, 1 1 Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. the write strength (beta) to 1, 2 2 After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. and using one-hot key encoding, 3 3 A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. every write we perform will overwrite exactly one row, and every one-hot query can retrieve an exact value. This means that the GDN layers themselves can work exactly as RAM, at a far lower cost than using normal attention as RAM, since a GDN head's state stays the same size however long the conversation gets, unlike attention's KV cache.

Gated DeltaNet state used as RAM: a one-hot key overwrites one row, a one-hot query reads it back, and the CPU keeps its registers, memory and program counter in those rows

The idea that the delta rule acts as a memory isn't new: Schlag et al. (2021) showed that linear attention with the delta rule works as an associative memory, or "fast weights". 4 4 Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, " Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers ", ICML 2021. The new thing here is making it exact and addressable, inside a production model, reliably enough to run a whole CPU on it.

This is the base on which this entire model is built. As it stands, default Qwen 3.5 does not keep exact values in the GDN. With this modification, we unlock the next part of this experiment.

Since we have a fully functional, cheap and fast RAM now, we can go ahead with compiling a working CPU into the model weights. Luckily, there's no training involved: a compiler sets every weight directly. You describe the CPU as a circuit, a long list of small steps like "read this register", "add these two numbers" or "jump if zero", and the compiler turns each step into a piece of a transformer layer: attention heads that look things up, feed-forward units that do the arithmetic, and DeltaNet heads that hold the RAM. The CPU then runs as the model decodes.

NetBSD 커널은 리눅스에 비해 하드웨어 지원이 고르지 않다. 패키지 관리자로 apk-tools와 busybox를 탑재하고, BSD make 대신 GNU make를 쓰는 등 GNU 계열 사용자 공간을 일부 채택했다. Alpine Linux의 포크가 아니며 패키지 모음은 독자적이지만 상당수 패키지는 aports에 기반한다. Alpine Linux는 OpenRC 초기화 시스템을 쓰는데, 본문은 AlpineBSD가 쓰는 초기화 방식을 설명하는 부분에서 잘려 있다.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Valve admits Steam has an AI slop and cloning problem, but says 'we don't want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn't use'
items.content:
(Image credit: Getty Images - Photo by Dilara Irem Sancar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The rise of AI slop is a real problem for Steam. Developers are growing wary of sharing their concepts and demos for fear of them being cloned , while Next Fest events meant to showcase upcoming games are being choked by literally thousands of demos hastily cranked out by 'developers' who are throwing everything imaginable at the wall in hopes that something will stick.

Speaking at the Steam Indie Connect event in Busan, South Korea, Valve's Tom Giardino and Marc Wilkinson acknowledged the problem, which as reported by Inven Global included at least one instance of a developer reporting extortion threats: "If you don't pay, we'll clone your game with AI and release it first." But the pair suggested that Valve isn't really in a position to do much about it, at least as far as regulating what is and isn't allowed on the platform. "We don't want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn't use," Giardino said.

Noting that games were being cloned long before AI came on the scene—just at a much slower pace—Giardino suggested that developers can protect their work by first building a strong community around it, and then focusing on continual improvements: "Rather than relying on a single mechanic that someone can easily copy, you need to keep growing your game by adding features, personality, and creativity that stem from your own perspective."

Valve's approach to the deluge of AI games flooding the Steam Next Fest is similar. Wilkinson said that during the first two days of the event, Steam users are shown games virtually randomly—but after that, the platform starts making personalized recommendations, showing users games they're more likely to enjoy. The goal of that early randomization, he explained, is to give every developer a fair shot at visibility, before drilling down into actual preferences.

"We recognize that the trade-off is some low-quality games get exposed," Wilkinson said. "We are fully aware of the situation, and a significant number of people are thinking about how to solve this problem."

It is a problem—this SteamDB chart of Steam game releases by year very clearly illustrates why:

(Image credit: SteamDB) Nearly 23,000 games have been released on Steam in 2026 alone, and it's not even November yet. Most of them are garbo, irrespective of the role AI played in their development, but it's still an incredible mass of videogames that users and developers alike have to wrestle with. It may not be an issue for major studios releasing big name games, but for the person plugging away on what might potentially be the next Animal Well, Balatro, or Vampire Survivors, the risk of being swept away in a flood of low-effort slop and clones is inescapable.

Israel Mallén of Digital Suns Games, which cancelled a planned Moonlighter demo on Steam over worries that it would be cloned, recently suggested that storefronts like Steam could help combat unethical game cloning by giving developers "more tools to vet who gets access [to pre-release builds], like account age, playtime or review history."

But while Valve is grappling with the problem, it doesn't sound like major changes of that sort are imminent: Giardino acknowledged that "there's plenty of room for improvement" but said, "Rather than limiting developer access, making Steam a smarter and more dynamic platform is the starting point of our philosophy."
