items.title: Amazon puts a camera in Echo Studio so Alexa can see what you hold up
items.content:
Amazon has put a camera in its Echo Studio speaker so that Alexa can see what is in front of it. The Echo Studio with Home Camera is one of five new Alexa devices the company unveiled on Wednesday , alongside a new Echo Dot, an Echo Time alarm clock, an Alexa Photo Frame and the Echo Show 16.

The camera speaker ships today for $249.99. Hold up a board game box and Alexa can explain the rules, or show it a box of cereal and it can help you reorder it, according to Amazon . Owners can also check in on the room from the Alexa app while they are away. The Echo Studio without a camera stays on sale at $219.99.

“The standard Echo Studio remains available for those who prefer no camera.” Amazon

A dedicated button turns off the microphones and any camera, and a visual indicator shows when a camera streams images or video to the cloud, Amazon said. Certain features require Alexa+, which is included with a Prime membership.

The new Echo Dot costs $99.99 and ships today. For the first time, it has a built-in smart home hub that supports Zigbee, Matter and Thread. It also includes an eero Wi-Fi extender that adds up to 1,000 square feet of coverage.

The Dot runs on Amazon’s custom AZ3 chip, with an AI accelerator for on-device processing. Two Amazon Kids versions cost from $109.99 with a year of Kids+.

Echo Time, a $199.99 alarm clock, has a 3.2-inch round touchscreen and no camera. It uses ultrasound to sense breathing and can wake its owner within 10 to 60 minutes of the set alarm, with no wearable needed. Sleep sensing is opt-in, Amazon said .

The Alexa Photo Frame has a 10-inch touchscreen and costs from $199.99. Alexa+ picks photos from Amazon Photos “based on faces, time, and sentiment”, and skips screenshots and receipts, according to Amazon .

The Echo Show 16 is available to preorder from $499.99, or $569.99 with an anti-glare Nanomatte screen. It ships later this year. It has a 13-megapixel wide-angle camera and, for the first time on an Echo Show, night vision. Fire TV is built in.

Echo Show is Amazon’s fastest-growing Echo product line, growing more than 25% year over year, the company said.

Amazon also announced Alexa Home Map , an interactive 3D view of the home built by scanning rooms with an iPhone. It shows devices, Ring and Blink cameras and a 360-degree aerial view of the property. A timeline can rewind the last 24 hours across all cameras.

Home Map starts rolling out in preview later this year on iOS, the Alexa and Ring apps, larger Echo Show devices and the new Alexa Tablets . Some features need a Ring Protect Pro or Virtual Security Guard subscription.

Hundreds of millions of customers are using the new Alexa experiences, Amazon said. The launches follow Amazon’s relaunch of Bee earlier this month and the device price rises it made in August.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

items.title: Secret FISA Ruling Allegedly Details Warrantless Searches of Americans’ Messages
items.content:
Secret FISA Ruling Allegedly Details Warrantless Searches of Americans’ Messages

A warrantless search by any other name still looks like a warrantless search.

If you’re tired of censorship and surveillance, subscribe to Reclaim The Net .

The US federal government is violating the law by keeping secret a March 17 ruling of the FISA Court regarding Section 702 surveillance, say two US senators.

The ruling accusation is about analysts reading Americans’ messages without a warrant. And that is something the public has a right to know about, say Democrats Ron Wyden and Adam Schiff.

The administration is keeping this information secret while at the same time asking Congress to renew the program.

The legal deadline to release the ruling was 180 days after it was issued, which was on September 13. The senators said that the opinion contains information about “serious abuses of Americans’ rights.”

The FISA Court found that the search filters used by the government to sift through intercepted data were not in line with the law, as they allowed analysts to access Americans’ messages without the necessary approvals, justifications, or records, according to a WIRED report .

The system in question was supposed to filter out US persons’ information, but instead it let analysts pull those communications out of the vast amounts of data collected under Section 702, which targets foreigners but inevitably also sweeps in Americans.

The court found that the tools the government uses to narrow down the data to Americans’ messages constitute a search of US persons, and ordered that the tools be rebuilt, the New York Times reported in April.

The Brennan Center for Justice, a non-profit, has now said that the ruling shows that problems that the Department of Justice (DOJ) said had been fixed as far back as early 2025 were still ongoing – and not only at the FBI, but across the entire intelligence community.

This is because the “self-policing” of the FBI and DOJ is not working, the center said.

In the past, the FBI used a tool to sift through the huge amounts of data collected under Section 702, and pull out communications of US persons, using what is known as a “participants filter” – which allowed agents to read messages of people in contact with the original foreign target, and do all this without a warrant.

This was first reported in 2025, when the Department of Justice told the FISA Court that the FBI had been running searches that were not logged. The FBI then turned off the tool, but switched it back on later that year.

FBI Director Kash Patel closed the Office of Internal Auditing last May. And the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board (PCLOB), the government’s own privacy watchdog, said that searches using the participants filter are “not possible to track.”

Wyden and Schiff have now sent a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche, to inform them that the deadline to release the FISA Court ruling has passed, and to demand that it be published as soon as possible.

We obtained a copy of the letter for you here .

They also want to know who is responsible for the delay, and want that information by November 6.

“As Congress continues to debate the fate of this authority, lawmakers must be able to discuss these abuses openly,” the two senators wrote. “Otherwise, the American people will rightly question whether a government that so flagrantly violates basic legal requirements, like the statute requiring declassification, can ever be trusted to not abuse a powerful surveillance tool like Section 702.”

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the letter reads, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

items.title: CNC Stone Carving
items.content:
In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place.  However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange.  To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head.

(The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.)

CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church.  Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days.  Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today.

The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth.  Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers.  The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God.

CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine.  The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts.  Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention.

Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone.  The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away.  The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process.

Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone.  “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion.  So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone.    Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues.  The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone.   CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight.  This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings!

The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy.  Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology.  With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen.  With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs.

The Prussiani machines also have a reputation of being indestructible, a reputation proven in the battlefield of stone carving.  Stone is an incalcitrant material, and it takes robust machines to subdue it; no small task!  Here’s a little story to illustrate.  For the first time, a few months after we started carving stone, we left our first CNC machine running overnight on several 7 foot long window sills.  We woke to a shocking surprise the following morning.  The huge stones, weighing several hundred pounds each, had been thrown about as if a tornado had ripped through the machine.  Stones were snapped and shattered, the fragments scattered about the…

items.title: GOTO Considered Totally Sick (for error handling in C)
items.content:
I recently started writing C again for the first time since 2018, and handling errors has been an especially difficult adjustment coming from languages like Go and Zig that coddle me with their wonderful defer and errdefer . Then I read some emails from John Carmack on inlined code that gave me an epiphany on writing cleaner error handling code, and now I want to share it with the world.

I write Go all day at my dayjob, and error handling is pretty trivial. When there’s an error we wrap it and bubble it up, and let some top dog up the call stack figure out what they want to do with it. If there is resource cleanup involved, it’s made easy with defer :

Sometimes there’s more complicated handling, but in 99% of scenarios it’s that simple because Go doesn’t have manual memory allocation and you don’t need to worry about cleaning it up when there’s an error.

Zig on the other hand does require you to manually manage memory, which I find a little more difficult because I’m not experienced enough for it to be second nature like it is when I write Go. Here’s a snippet from my toy multiplexer that uses errdefer :

I’m allocating memory for several types, and because any one of the allocations can fail I need to handle freeing up each succesful memory allocation that preceded the failure. Zig’s errdefer makes this easy, there’s no manual tracking of what needs to be freed at any point, because the deferred statements will execute in reverse order if the function returns an error. Also I’m following the Reserve First pattern, which is where I learned errdefer comptime unreachable from.

Now, enter C. There’s no defer or errdefer . I’ve painted myself into a corner with some ugly code a few times because I’m so used to those tools that I don’t regularly plan ahead for what my error handling control flow will look like. Until recently I’ve been writing code that looks like this:

Do you see how resource cleanup is slightly different across each error handling if-block? Yuck! Yeah yeah yeah, I know it’s a terrible, contrived example, and nobody would ever write C like this. Except me like 3 weeks ago. I knew something was wrong when I wrote code like this, but I was hopelessly defer -brained in a world where defer hadn’t been born yet. Some classmates had mentioned using goto but I couldn’t really wrap my head around it. (We can’t share code with eachother otherwise the university would have us killed).

Then when I read those John Carmack emails something clicked. Carmack doesn’t mention goto explicitly, but these two thoughts in particular were the special sauce I needed to help me understand (emphasis mine):

A quote from Henry Spencer describing control flow in some flight software:

It disallowed both subroutine calls and backward branches, except for the one at the bottom of the main loop. Control flow went forward only . Sometimes one piece of code had to leave a note for a later piece telling it what to do, but this worked out well for testing: all data was allocated statically, and monitoring those variables gave a clear picture of most everything the software was doing.

And Carmack on moving code out of large conditional blocks (emphasis mine):

Enclosing pages of code inside a conditional or loop statement does have readability and awareness drawbacks, so leaving that code in a separate function may still be justified, but in some cases it is still possible to move the code to another place where its execution wouldn’t be conditional , or just execute it at all times and inhibit the results in some way with a very small conditional block.

Ohmygodigetitnow. Instead of having multiple exit points scattered throughout my function, each performing their own resource cleanup, I can put all resource cleanup behind a single exit point at the very end of the function. Guarding cleanup behind the default return, only reachable using a goto , is kinda like a psuedo- errdefer . Hooray! Hooray for John Carmack and Henry Spencer!! Now…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: 'Minnesota 15' Case Reveals Largest US Government Spying on Left Since COINTELPRO
items.content:
Brett Wilkins Brett Wilkins is a staff writer for Common Dreams.

The Trump administration is conducting what some experts believe is the largest government surveillance campaign targeting American leftists in over half a century, deploying undercover agents, drones, financial investigators, and digital monitoring against opponents of President Donald Trump’s deadly immigration crackdown, according to reporting published Wednesday.

Wired reporter Ali Winston examined court records regarding the prosecution of the so-called " Minnesota 15 ," a group of activists facing federal conspiracy charges after organizing and taking part in protests and other resistance to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) deadly Operation Metro Surge crackdown in the Twin Cities.

The Minnesota 15 are members of the groups Direct Action Minnesota and Black Cat Workers , and are accused of impeding the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) anti-immigrant crackdown in Minneapolis, where US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti were separately killed earlier this year by ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers and where Julio César Sosa-Celis survived being shot by an ICE agent.

Winston's investigation centers on Operation Puppet Master and Project Whipple Shield , probes conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of ICE. More than 120 HSI agents were assigned to the Minnesota campaigns, including at least 11 undercover operatives who infiltrated activist meetings, marches, training sessions, and encrypted Signal chats.

Those operations were authorized under National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7), which was signed by Trump following last year’s assassination of Charlie Kirk in an effort to target the left—even though leftists had nothing to do with the racist influencer's murder.

Federal agents also spied on gatherings in other states, photographed vehicles, deployed unarmed Reaper drones, and examined activists' digital records and financial transactions.

Civil liberties advocates and former law enforcement officials said the campaign evokes the Federal Bureau of Investigation's notorious COINTELPRO program, which surveilled, infiltrated, and sought to disrupt Civil Rights , Black liberation, anti-war, American Indian, and other movements during the tenure of FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover—including by funding and arming murderous far-right militants to terrorize leftists.

According to a 2011 book by former [Central Intelligence Agency] officer Frank Rafalko , the CIA secret investigation into suspected foreign influence on the New Left and anti-Vietnam War movement had 42 officers working the case at its peak. Court records show 119 HSI agents worked on the Minnesota 15 case alone.

“Broad monitoring of social media , communications, and financial transactions are used to link an ever-increasing number of people as potential subjects of investigation and prosecution,” Mike German, a retired FBI agent critical of the post-9/11 surveillance state, told Winston. “These are exactly the kind of intelligence activities J. Edgar Hoover adopted to suppress the Civil Rights and anti-war movements in the 1960s.”

'Major Escalation': Trump Prosecutor Invokes NSPM-7 While Unveiling Charges Against 15 ICE Protesters ›

Marking One Year of NSPM-7, Rights Advocates Call On Congress to Rein In FBI's Spying Capabilities ›

items.title: CSS-Tricks has a new owner!
items.content:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle.

This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news:

CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again!

Just to recap:  DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022  from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase.

Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site.

So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have  a small, awesome team  to help with the day-to-day management of the site.

That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion.

Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while.

I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of  everyone , no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.

My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right.

It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently.

In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots.

So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise,  please do reach out !

Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners.

(And you can now support the site by becoming a member  — thanks in advance!)

Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as  our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap .

And yes, I do believe that  learning the basics is more important now than ever . But what learning actually looks like is what’s key. Front-end courses are  down across the board . It has to be done differently.

There are other things in the works, but I think a course is one of the first things you’ll see.

Oh, and  the newsletter . That’s coming back after a way-too-long hiatus.

That’s still very much a thing! We’ll keep our regularly scheduled broadcast going.

But maybe a little less than you’re used to. Those articles are part of the investment I’m making. Expect maybe one or two articles most weeks, at least as the ball starts rolling.

That also means the  guest writing form  is back in business! We have a nice backlog of articles through the rest of the year, which is great, but also means new submissions will have to wait a bit.

I won’t be able to accept everything that comes in, but I will absolutely read them and follow-up as best I can.  Unless it’s a slop submission , of course.

Will you be writing most of the articles to save cost?

Nah! My goal is to make CSS-Tricks a platform that gives folks a voice to share great ideas. I think we all prefer that over me just using it as my own soapbox. I’ve written plenty for this site the past 12 years. I’m happier (and more comfortable) being behind the curtain and giving others the full spotlight.

I may be writing a bit, developing the site here and there, editing a small stack of article drafts, or…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

제가 보기에는 블랙해커들 보다는 서버측이 클라이언트의 행동을 분석하는 과정처럼 보이더군요..

items.title: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model
items.content:
Claude Code burns ~15–20% of your tokens on a 3-word status line. Here's how to turn it off

Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312 (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified ( BUN_OPTIONS=--preload ). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify.

curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce/raw/no-agent-summary.js -o ~ /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js

BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload $HOME /.local/share/no-agent-summary.js " claude

To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install .

Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire

transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent

action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it

never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since

2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default.

The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export:

grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself .

Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate ( cost_usd ), not an invoice: on a

subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it:

no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~80 lines of code). It wraps setTimeout / setInterval ;

when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired

log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes

through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are

claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary .

Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so

editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a

wrapped globalThis.fetch . But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source

even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert

timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay

Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path.

Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. One of:

export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js "

set -gx BUN_OPTIONS " --preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js "

# ~/.config/environment.d/50-no-agent-summary.conf (systemd user env; also reaches

# user services and timers; applies when the user manager next starts, usually next login)

BUN_OPTIONS =--preload /abs/path/no-agent-summary.js

Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude

* ) export BUN_OPTIONS= " ${BUN_OPTIONS : + $BUN_OPTIONS } --preload $HOOK " ;;

: " ${CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG := ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR :-/ tmp} / no-agent-summary.log} "

Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an

off suppresses the summary timer. pass is the A/B control: loads and logs, arms every timer untouched. Any other value warns on stderr and acts as off .

Appends preload active mode=… bun=… hooked=… on load, one line per matched timer (first 20), and an exit count.

Overwritten on load with the preload active … line.

Restart the daemon after install. The daemon, pty host and pre-warmed bg-spare sessions

inherit the environment of the client that started the daemon, so a daemon started before

BUN_OPTIONS was set keeps spawning unhooked sessions. Hence claude daemon stop --any .

Headless runs need it too: claude -p , cron, CI, editor integrations.

Platform: Linux tested, macOS and Windows untested. On Windows the /$bunfs/ gate most

items.title: The case of the 9 bit AES key
items.content:
We found that several PDF implementations generate their AES-256 file keys from state spaces small enough to enumerate. In MuPDF, only 9 bits of random state affect the actual AES-256 key. Other PDF editors like Foxit base their AES-256 key on time based randomness and thus also lead to keys that are trivial to recover.

PDF encryption protects the strings and datastreams in a PDF document, including metadata unless it is explicitly left unencrypted. The password protection mechanism has gone through a bunch of revisions over the years, moving from RC4 to AES and hardening password hashing against brute force attacks. The current version, revision 6, uses AES-256.

When a PDF is encrypted with AES-256, the password does not encrypt the document directly. The implementation generates a random 32-byte file key, which encrypts the content. The password and a salt are then hashed to derive a separate key, which encrypts this random 32-byte file key. Revision 6 makes this hashing deliberately slow; the older AES-256 revision 5 does not.

A PDF can have a user password for viewing and an owner password for changing permissions. Either unlocks the same file key, so the restrictions are up to the reader: with the viewing password, you can also make an unrestricted copy.

We found that this randomness is often generated very insecurely, allowing passwordless decryption of protected PDFs.

MuPDF versions before 1.28.5 use an implementation of the drand48 family to generate their random numbers. This generator is seeded once, using the current epoch in seconds:

static void fz_init_random_context ( fz_context * ctx )

fz_srand48 ( ctx , ( uint32_t ) time ( NULL ));

The generator is a 48-bit linear congruential generator:

s n + 1 = ( 𝟶 𝚡 𝟻 𝚍 𝚎 𝚎 𝚌 𝚎 𝟼𝟼 𝚍 s n + 𝟶 𝚡 𝚋 ) mod 2 48

fz_srand48() writes the state as three 16-bit words. The low word is the constant 0x330e , and the 32-bit timestamp occupies state bits 16 to 47:

void fz_srand48 ( fz_context * ctx , int32_t seed )

uint16_t p [ 3 ] = { 0x 330e , seed , seed >> 16 };

When MuPDF needs to generate a key, it calls fz_memrnd() , which will repeatedly take a random number, step the random number generator forward, and then use the lowest byte of this random number as a random byte.

int32_t fz_nrand48 ( fz_context * ctx , uint16_t s [ 3 ])

return fz_rand48_step ( s , ctx -> seed48 + 3 ) >> 17 ;

* data ++ = ( unsigned char ) fz_lrand48 ( ctx );

seed48+3) >> 17;}/* in fz_memrnd() */while (len-- > 0) *data++ = (unsigned char)fz_lrand48(ctx);">

The shift discards state bits 0 to 16, and the cast to unsigned char discards everything above bit 24. Every output byte therefore comes from bits 17 to 24 of the LCG state.

The issue is that the higher bits of the state never affect the lower bits. Multiplication and addition can carry bits upward, but not downward. Since each output byte comes from bits 17 to 24, anything above bit 24 can be ignored, even after stepping the generator forward.

That leaves 25 bits that can affect the output. The bottom 16 are always initialized to 0x330e , so only nine bits from the timestamp matter. Timestamps that differ by 512 seconds produce exactly the same byte stream.

Since the possible keyspace is so small, we can just brute-force this by generating all possible 32-byte keys and trial decrypting:

state = ( 0x 5deece66d * state + 0x b ) & (( 1 << 48 ) - 1 )

candidates = [ stream ( seed , 64 )[ 32 : 64 ] for seed in range ( 512 )]

> 17) & 0xff) return bytes(out)candidates = [stream(seed, 64)[32:64] for seed in range(512)]">

MuPDF uses the same generator for the document /ID , which is stored in the trailer in plaintext. When writing a new document, it will first draw 32 bytes from the same LCG and then immediately sample the decryption key after, so /ID can be used as an additional check.

items.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections: But the AI responses get more forthright when asked outside the US.
items.content:
If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden’s win that November. If you ask Google’s AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources.

When I put the direct question of “Who won the 2020 presidential election?” to Google’s AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media ), I got the following surprisingly indirect response:

“To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC).”

My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google’s AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project’s 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000.

If I just wanted a link I wouldn’t have used AI mode…

If I just wanted a link I wouldn’t have used AI mode…

Other Ars staffers found that AI Mode would similarly provide direct answers to some presidential result questions but not others. The specific election cycles that received each type of response seemed to differ by individual user, though; one staffer reported only getting immediate answers from AI Mode when asking about the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, with others going back to 2000 simply providing links to outside data.

The oddities continued when I tested some other political history questions in Google’s AI Mode. When asked which party controlled the Senate after the 2020 elections, for instance, Google’s AI Mode told me to “check official congressional records” and linked me to the US Senate Party Division history page . When asked the same question for 1992 election, though, AI Mode simply told me straight out that it led to Democrats holding a 57 to 43 majority in the Senate, including Wikipedia among its references.

Did AI Mode suffer a concussion somewhere between 1992 and 2020?

Did AI Mode suffer a concussion somewhere between 1992 and 2020?

Separate from Google’s AI Mode, the company’s own Gemini model seems perfectly capable of telling me who won recent presidential elections. The same goes for other major chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and even the government-run AI model at America.gov .

Perhaps tellingly, Google AI Mode’s issues with providing direct answers on presidential results seemed to disappear when accessing Google’s AI Mode in foreign countries. Spot checks via VPN of AI Mode results accessed from Taiwan, Russia, France, and Canada all got accurate and straightforward answers to multiple questions about recent US election results.

Google’s AI Mode also seems to grow more accommodating when the same political questions are asked a second time. After repeating questions about presidential results, AI Mode actually told me the winner for all three elections where it had previously only provided outside links, citing Google Civics data in the latter response.

When asked why it didn’t provide that kind of immediate answer the first time, Google’s AI Mode blamed “safety filters for recent and highly sensitive election topics [that] are very strict.” For recent elections or those involving active political figures, AI Mode says its “system is heavily automated to direct users directly to official, certified government databases—like the Federal Election Commission—to prevent any risk of displaying unverified data or misinformation.”

items.title: ICE is running one of the largest anti-left surveilance operations in US History
items.content:
Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond.

The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities.

Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s.

Among the records revealed during the discovery process in these cases are dozens of reports, audio transcripts, emails, intercepted Signal chats, photographs, database queries, and more. They reveal the inner workings of the domestic terrorism investigations, running under the names Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master, authorized by the controversial National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 .

Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people who criticize the administration's policies and espouse "anti-Christian" ideas. The full scope and extent of the investigations it authorizes remains unknown.

Defense attorneys for the Minnesota 15 claim that the prosecution stems from a broader nationwide surveillance operation aimed at opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. One attorney in the case directly compares the DHS-run campaign to the FBI’s infamous Counterintelligence Program, or COINTELPRO, which unconstitutionally surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed racial justice, civil rights, and anti-war movements from the 1950s through the early 1970s.

Three former law enforcement officials who reviewed filings concur, telling WIRED that the case is almost certainly part of a wider intelligence-gathering operation that began long before the administration invaded Minnesota in December 2025.

Dueling motions in the case over discovery of DHS’s surveillance program reveal that personnel with Homeland Security Investigations—one of ICE’s two components—repurposed funding mechanisms and investigative tools for serious criminal probes and turned them on domestic dissenters. Operation Keyhole, the HSI undercover program that bankrolled the Minnesota 15 prosecution, dates back to 2008. As of June 2026, it was underwriting a half dozen active undercover investigations in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area.

Around 120 HSI agents, many drawn from specialized units across the country that have served as the leading edge of the administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations, were assigned to the case—including 11 undercovers. They used highly invasive surveillance techniques, including the deployment of Reaper drones and Patriot Act tools usually restricted to money laundering and terrorism investigations. Undercover operatives also infiltrated churches in apparent violation of a court order.

The Minnesota 15 indictment stems from the Trump administration’s demand that the Justice Department “go big and go loud” to crack down on community response networks during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge. Twin Cities activists organized volunteers to monitor DHS agents and their vehicles using encrypted Signal groups, homebuilt vehicle databases, and a centralized dispatch system. Government prosecutors claim that this amounts to a criminal conspiracy to block immigration enforcement, unlawfully identify and stalk federal agents, and even assault them.

items.title: A Health Update
items.content:
I’m writing this post from a hospital bed. And I couldn’t be happier.

You hear folks say chemotherapy sucks, but until you go through it yourself, you don’t really know how bad it can be. It remains a popular activity only because it’s better than the alternative.

My first exposure to chemotherapy was with this contraption: a fluoroscope.

Lovely to look at, less lovely to lie on.

Every week, they used this machine to tap into my spine, extract 5 mg of fluid for analysis, and replace it with 5 mg of methotrexate . There was only a local anesthetic during the procedure and the hardest part was knowing that there was a needle, turned up to eleven, going into my back.

It was afterwards that things got dicey: the nerves in your spine float in a thecal sac filled with spinal fluid that acts as a kind of insulator. Since we were exchanging the fluids, it was easy for the levels to get out of balance and for the nerves to react.

The result were the worst headaches I’ve ever experienced. The good news is that the remedy was simple: to lie flat on my back to ease the pressure gravity was putting on my spine.

That was also the bad news: many days were spent lying prone and trying to avoid boredom. Watching shows and scrolling timelines just doesn’t cut it when that’s all you can do.

Thankfully, the spinal headaches subsided quickly when the six-week course of lumbar punctures finished at the end of January. But my body began to face a new challenge: chemotherapy infusions of Bendamustine and Rituximab .

Everyone experiences chemotherapy differently. Just as every body is different, so is the reaction to the chemicals that are killing the cancer.

The first effect I noticed was in my tastebuds: everything I put in my mouth had a slightly metalic taste, so my eating habits changed. My beloved morning coffee was replaced by tea, food needed a lot less salt, and I started eating a blander diet (cottage cheese with berries remains a favorite).

Some people experience nausea and other gastric issues: luckily, I avoided that. I also didn’t have any hair loss, but my normally thick and curly hair lost its body and became lifeless: an external expression of what was happening to me internally.

As someone who’s always been active and strong, the biggest overall effect of chemo was losing muscle mass and suffering from overall fatigue. It felt very strange to be weak.

I was on a 28 day cycle for my infusions: during the first week I got pumped full of chemicals and then spent three weeks letting my body process them. One of the things they gave me with the infusion on a Tuesday was a dose of steroids that gives the body a boost during the initial onslaught. But by the weekend, that wore off and I felt like shit. It usually took until the middle of the second week before I started feeling human again.

I didn’t lose my appetite, but I wasn’t eating more than normal. The problem was my metabolism was working overtime and my calorie intake didn’t adjust. I lost 50 pounds over the course of a couple of months and eventually got to the point where I was having five meals a day. Too bad it all tasted bad.

This could also be a graph of my happiness.

One thing that I did to fight my diminished capacity was a daily walk. Anyone who exercises regularly knows that there are always plenty of reasons to avoid it: you didn’t sleep well, you have an important project to finish, or you’re sore from a previous workout. When you’re doing chemo, add feeling like absolute shit to that list.

I still had nerve damage in my spine, so my “walk” was more like a shuffle. Thankfully my wife found some awesome walking sticks to aid with my balance. They are clearly labelled “Not A Medical Device” but they are my most important medical device.

Winter sunsets, exercise, and walking sticks are good medicine.

My daily exercise was just like any gym workout: dread at the start, joy at the end. Sometimes there wasn’t much behind that joy: at my lowest point, a walk…

items.title: The Future Trait Has A Missing State
items.content:
In async Rust the Future::poll method is called to progress the state of the future, which reports its progress via the Poll enum. This enum contains two variants:

Poll::Pending : means that the future is not yet ready to produce a value, and poll will need to be invoked again later.

Poll::Ready(T) : means the future is ready to yield some value T .

Futures are called that because they will eventually resolve to a value, in the future . But that’s value singular, not values plural. The stdlib documentation does not clearly make this guarantee (though it should), and the ecosystem doesn’t always implement this correctly (though it also should). But the intent is clear: one future should only ever yield one value.

Now what should happen when you try and call Future::poll again after it has already yielded a value? The Future trait docs have the following to say:

Once a future has completed (returned Ready from poll ), calling its poll method again may panic, block forever, or cause other kinds of problems; the Future trait places no requirements on the effects of such a call. However, as the poll method is not marked unsafe , Rust’s usual rules apply […].

The docs state here that if you call Future::poll again after it’s yielded

Poll::Ready , that’s unsupported and there aren’t many limits on the future’s

behavior. The most common behavior here is to panic! , which is the behavior

for all async blocks and functions. Which is a shame, since being able to call

Future::poll again after it’s yielded Ready before is actually quite useful

and something I frequently wish I was able to do.

Not everyone writing Rust writes async Rust, and not everyone writing async Rust will write async concurrency primitives. But those who do will be familiar with the MaybeDone type. It’s a simple wrapper around some Future whose only job it is to either hold a Future or if it's completed hold its Future::Output . While not simple, assuming you're familiar enough with async Rust it should be easy enough to follow:

# [ pin_project ( project = DoneState )]

pub fn take ( self : Pin < & mut Self >) -> Option < F :: Output > {

DoneState :: Done ( output ) => output . take (),

impl < F : Future > Future for MaybeDone < F > {

fn poll ( mut self : Pin < & mut Self >, cx : & mut Context < ' _ >) -> Poll <()> {

DoneState :: Future ( future ) => match future . poll ( cx ) {

self . set ( Self :: Done ( Some ( output )));

DoneState :: Done ( _ ) => Poll :: Ready (()),

In essence what this provides is a slot that holds either a future, or its final resolved value. And in doing so it also performs another trick: it replaces the output of the future with the unit type and adds a new method take to actually extract the value of the future.

When attempting to call Future::poll again after it has returned Poll::Ready(()) once before, it will always continue to return Poll::Ready(()) . And if you call the take method again after having received Some(Future::Output) before, it will keep returning None forever after.

What is a relatively straightforward way of creating a slot that holds either a future or its output value has an interesting side effect of actually being able to communicate the state of the future even after it has yielded a value once. If a caller observes Poll::Ready(()) + None , that means the future is done and will not be yielding a value again.

MaybeDone isn’t the only API in the futures crate which tracks the done state of a

future. The FusedFuture trait provides an is_terminated method, and its Fuse

adapter keeps returning Poll::Pending once the inner future has returned

Poll::Ready . However this unfortunately abuses Poll::Pending , whose docs state:

When a function returns Pending , the function must also ensure that the current task is scheduled to be awoken when progress can be made.

This definition is incompatible with how Fuse uses Pending , and so bringing

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Nim version 2.4.0 released
items.content:
The Nim Team is happy to announce version 2.4.0, our new stable release.

After a way-too-long period of development, Nim 2.4 has finally become a reality. This is a major update

If you’re still on Nim 1.6, take a look at the version 2.0 release article to see all the features you’re missing.

If you’ve been using Nim 2.0, the version 2.2 release article shows the improvements available in Nim 2.2.

If you want to stay on Nim 2.2 for now, we also released version 2.2.14 today, a patch release with many bugfixes and security fixes.

Check out if the package manager of your OS already ships version 2.4.0 or

If you have installed a previous version of Nim using choosenim ,

NOTE: We recommend that you install and use the latest version of choosenim , v0.8.16, available in our choosenim repo .

Alternatively, you can download Nim 2.4.0 from

SSO-based strings come with a new low-level strings API that you have to use in order to use this switch effectively.

Nim’s new strings API is compatible with Nimony’s, so porting is always beneficial, even if --strings:sso might not improve the performance of your code.

See it as a worthwhile, future-proof refactoring in its own right.

The general idea behind this API is to deprecate the operation addr myString[offset] and to replace it with operations that clarify the intent . Reading

Because the helper API has identical signatures on every string backend, code

written this way keeps working under refc/ARC/ORC without SSO; you can port

incrementally and flip --strings:sso on when ready.

Updating your code is not required, but beneficial. The new API works for all mm switches and is also offered by Nimony/Nim 3.

IC is finally shipping! Use it with the switch --ic:on . Parallel builds are based on multi-processing, not multi-threading. Hence macros that make use of global .compileTime variables might need to get patched before you can enjoy the benefits of much faster rebuilds.

For an example of the required porting effort, see my PR here that allows PolyWorld to be built with --ic:on !

Depending on the shape of your import graphs, even cold builds might be faster with IC turned on, as the build exploits more parallelism. For example, compiling the Nim compiler itself takes 31s with --ic:off on a machine with 16 physical cores, and 25s with --ic:on .

YRC (“ürk”) is the thread-safe variant of Nim’s ORC. Use --mm:yrc when you need shared refs and cycles across threads. It offers the same API as ORC. Where it fits:

ORC can only handle cycles that stay inside one thread. YRC lifts that: cycles can span threads. For acyclic data it uses atomic reference counting; for cyclic data it uses a write barrier that only runs at pointer assignments. There is no stop-the-world phase and no arbitrary safepoints. Any thread can run the cycle collector when needed (there is no dedicated GC thread), which helps locality and suits embedded systems where every thread counts.

Nothing is free. In our orcbench, YRC is about 2.0× slower than ORC and it uses twice as much memory, too. Still, we think that’s a good trade: you no longer have to worry about cycles crossing thread boundaries. The cost is a constant factor of two; the payoff grows with every core you put to work on shared data.

items.title_ko: Nim 2.4.0 정식 출시
items.summary_ko: Nim 팀이 안정 버전 Nim 2.4.0을 발표했다. 긴 개발 기간을 거친 주요 업데이트이며, 같은 날 여러 버그와 보안 문제를 고친 2.2.14 패치 릴리스도 함께 나왔다. 입력 본문이 중간에서 끊겨 있어 세부 변경 사항은 확인할 수 없다.
items.content_ko: Nim 팀이 안정 버전 Nim 2.4.0을 발표했다. 긴 개발 기간 끝에 나온 주요 업데이트다. Nim 1.6을 쓰고 있다면 2.0 릴리스 글을, Nim 2.0을 쓰고 있다면 2.2 릴리스 글을 참고하라고 안내했다. Nim 2.2를 계속 쓰고 싶다면 많은 버그 수정과 보안 수정을 담은 2.2.14 패치 릴리스도 같은 날 나왔다. 새 기능으로는 SSO 기반 문자열(--strings:sso 스위치)과 이를 효과적으로 쓰기 위한 새 저수준 strings API가 소개되었다. 새 strings API는 Nimony와 호환되므로, --strings:sso로 성능이 크게 오르지 않더라도 이식해 두면 앞으로 도움이 된다고 설명했다. OS 패키지 관리자가 2.4.0을 제공하는지 확인하거나, choosenim으로 설치하는 방법을 안내하며, choosenim은 최신 버전 v0.8.16 사용을 권장했다. 본문은 중간에서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: 사생활침해 범죄가 의심 됩니다. 도움이 필요합니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-91153 📢 Source: Wordfence 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False The Everest Forms – Contact Form, Payment Form, Quiz, Survey & Custom Form Builder with AI plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Sensitive Information Exposure in all versions up to, and including, 3.6.2 via the process. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to extract arbitrary WordPress post meta values — including license keys, API tokens, SMTP credentials, and Stripe or AWS secrets stored on any post type — via form submission notification emails or stored entries. The submission nonce is publicly rendered in every embedded form and can additionally be minted anonymously via the nopriv everest_forms_get_form_update_nonce action, meaning no account or prior authentication of any kind is required to complete the exploit. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-29T09:25:36.385Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-91153

items.summary_ko: WordPress 플러그인 Everest Forms – Contact Form, Payment Form, Quiz, Survey & Custom Form Builder with AI의 3.6.2 이하 모든 버전에 민감 정보 노출 취약점이 있다. 인증되지 않은 공격자가 폼 제출 알림 이메일이나 저장된 항목을 통해 라이선스 키, API 토큰, SMTP 자격 증명, Stripe·AWS 시크릿 등 게시물 메타 값을 빼낼 수 있다. 피드에는 원격 악용 가능 여부가 False, CVSS 점수는 0.0(NA)으로 표기되어 있으나, 설명상 인증 없이도 공격이 가능하다고 되어 있어 표기와 설명이 일치하지 않는다.
items.content_ko: WordPress 플러그인 Everest Forms – Contact Form, Payment Form, Quiz, Survey & Custom Form Builder with AI는 3.6.2 버전까지 포함한 모든 버전에서 민감 정보 노출(Sensitive Information Exposure) 취약점이 있다. 인증되지 않은 공격자가 폼 제출 알림 이메일이나 저장된 항목을 통해 임의의 WordPress 게시물 메타 값을 추출할 수 있으며, 여기에는 라이선스 키, API 토큰, SMTP 자격 증명, Stripe나 AWS 시크릿이 포함될 수 있다. 제출 nonce는 삽입된 모든 폼에 공개되어 있고, nopriv everest_forms_get_form_update_nonce 액션으로 익명으로도 발급받을 수 있어, 공격에 계정이나 사전 인증이 필요하지 않다고 설명되어 있다. 피드 정보: 출처 Wordfence, CVSS 점수 0.0(NA), 원격 악용 가능 여부 False. 다만 이 원격 악용 가능 여부 표기는 위 설명과 맞지 않는다. 공개일은 2026년 10월 29일(UTC 기준 09:25:36)이다.
